reason: The multiverse combines different red-card outcomes, event/exposure estimands, and skin-tone representations. These choices define substantively different claims, especially because some specifications use continuous or multi-level skin-tone predictors rather than a direct dark-versus-light contrast.
parent_hypothesis: Referees are more likely to award red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned players.
dimensions: Outcome definition: all sendings-off versus straight red cards only
Event/exposure estimand: count rate, any-event probability, versus exposure-adjusted event rate
Skin-tone measurement and encoding: binary dark-versus-light versus continuous or five-level representations

hypotheses.hypothesis: Among player–referee dyads in the dataset, the probability of at least one sending-off (including second-yellow sendings-off) is higher for dark-skinned than for light-skinned players, using a prespecified binary skin-tone threshold and a dyad-level any-event logistic model.
hypotheses.rationale: The parent conflates any sending-off with straight red cards and also leaves the event estimand and skin-tone encoding open. Outcome choice changed inference in 51.6% of paired specifications, and the any-event model is a distinct probability estimand. Binary encoding is fixed because the parent states a dark-versus-light contrast. Covariate adjustment is also pinned because it produced large effect changes and inference flips; the remaining analytic choices are fixed to define one reproducible target rather than treated as additional forks.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Among player–referee dyads in the dataset, the probability of at least one straight red card is higher for dark-skinned than for light-skinned players, using a prespecified binary skin-tone threshold and a dyad-level any-event logistic model.
hypotheses.rationale: Straight red cards are substantively different from all sendings-off, and the two outcome definitions produced different inference in 51.6% of paired specifications without reversing the estimated sign. This successor therefore isolates the straight-red outcome while fixing the binary contrast, event estimand, and adjustment choices that otherwise leave the parent ambiguous.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Among players in the dataset, the exposure-adjusted rate of all sendings-off is higher for dark-skinned than for light-skinned players, using a prespecified binary skin-tone threshold and a Poisson exposure model.
hypotheses.rationale: An exposure-adjusted event rate is a different estimand from the probability that a dyad has any event. Count-rate, any-event, and Poisson exposure specifications showed materially different effect magnitudes and inference changes, so the rate claim must be separated rather than combined with the probability claims. The binary skin-tone contrast and covariate adjustment are fixed because their alternatives also materially altered results.
